[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/dModverse/dMod2/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dModverse/dMod2/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)

dMod2 builds ODE models of reaction networks, generates and compiles C++ code for them, and estimates their parameters from data. Prediction, observation, parameter transformation and objective functions return gradient and Hessian with their value, propagated forward or in one reverse sweep.

The [website](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/) has the reference, the example projects and a [guide](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/guide-model.html) from the setup of a model to fits, profile likelihoods and mixed effects.

## System requirements

Model code is generated and compiled at run time, so **C and C++ compilers** and **Python with SymPy** are required; reticulate provides the Python packages on first use. On Linux the compilers are usually present, Windows users need [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/). The default backend is [cppDE](https://github.com/dModverse/cppDE), which generates C++ with forward and reverse derivatives to second order; [cOde](https://github.com/dkaschek/cOde) with deSolve is available as an alternative.

## Installation

```r
remotes::install_github("dModverse/dMod2")
```

The backend [cppDE](https://github.com/dModverse/cppDE) comes along as a
`Remotes:` dependency and does not have to be installed separately.

### As an RStudio project

Working on the package itself is easier from a checkout.

1.  **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**, repository URL
    `https://github.com/dModverse/dMod2`.

2.  Install the dependencies, including the ones declared under `Remotes:`:

    ```r
    remotes::install_deps(dependencies = TRUE)
    ```

3.  **Build → Install and Restart**.

`cppDE` installs the same way and has to be built first: dMod2 compiles the
generated model sources against its headers.

## Building a model

Models are assembled from four kinds of function objects that compose with `*` (concatenation, chain rule) and `+` (direct sum over experimental conditions):

| Object | Constructor | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `odemodel`, `prdfn` | `odemodel()`, `Xs()` | the compiled ODE and its sensitivities |
| `obsfn` | `Y()` | observation and error functions |
| `parfn` | `P()` | parameter transformations |
| `objfn` | `normL2()`, `constraintL2()` | objective functions |

Four models are worked through end to end:

- [NFκB signalling after TNFα](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018.html): the model of
  [Oppelt et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41540-018-0058-z), 38 reactions in two
  compartments from a numerically computed resting state, its symmetries, a multistart, the
  reduction by profile likelihoods to a model whose parameters are all determined, a prediction
  band, and the changes five liver-toxic drugs cause, by spike-and-slab random effects. The
  guide goes through it.
- [JAK2-STAT5 signalling with feedbacks](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/bachmannMSB2011.html): the model of
  [Bachmann et al. (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1038/msb.2011.50), with 25 states
  in two compartments, the negative feedbacks CIS, SOCS3 and SHP1, and 113
  parameters estimated from 541 measurements across thirteen experiments, and its
  problem in PEtab.
- [STAT5 dimerisation after Epo stimulation](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/boehmJProteomeRes2014.html): the model of
  Boehm et al. (2014) from reactions to profile likelihoods, with a multistart
  fit, an error model by restricted maximum likelihood and confidence
  intervals.
- [IFN-alpha sensitization](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/kokMSB2020.html): the model of
  [Kok et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.15252/msb.20198955), its structural
  identifiability, the fit at the published optimum over 25 conditions, the
  gradient by forward sensitivities and by the reverse sweep, and the
  sensitization of a second dose by a first.

All four are example projects in [`examples/`](https://github.com/dModverse/dMod2/tree/master/examples)
of the repository, each with its data, scripts and saved results, as are [bile acid
transport](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/bileAcidTransport.html) from profile likelihoods to a prediction band, and
a [Hodgkin-Huxley neuron](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/hodgkinHuxleyJPhysiol1952.html) with switches on time and
state.

## Mixed-effects models

Random effects are written as effect formulas on the parameter transformation, in
the notation of lme4, and `em()` fits them by marginal maximum likelihood: FOCEI,
adaptive sparse-grid quadrature, laplaceEM or SAEM. Besides normal random effects,
Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process ones select which groups differ, with
their hyperparameters estimated in the same fit. The example projects show
[pharmacometric models](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/pharmacometrics.html) of theophylline, warfarin and mavoglurant
against nlmixr2 and a simulated [target-mediated drug disposition](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/TMDD.html); the guide
finds [which rates of NFκB signalling five drugs change](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/guide-group-effects.html) with
spike-and-slab random effects and [aligns](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/guide-alignment.html) qPCR experiments and Western blots with a
random gel background together with targeted mass spectrometry in nM with `align()`.

## Structural identifiability

`symmetryDetection()` finds the directions in parameters and initial values along
which the observations of a model do not change, and `symmetryReduction()` turns
them into a parameter transformation that removes them. Both run in the Python
package [symident](https://github.com/dModverse/symident), which dMod2 installs
from PyPI on first use; under `RETICULATE_PYTHON` install it there with
`pip install symident`. A steady-state start on coupled steady states needs
msolve, which `symmetryDetection()` offers to build when it is missing, or which
`SYMIDENT_MSOLVE` points to.

## Distributed computing

`distributedComputing()` runs fits, profiles or any other R code as tasks in the
background: on the local machine, on machines reached by ssh with the cores each may
use, or as an array job of a SLURM cluster through a job script template. The
[guide](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/articles/guide-remote-computing.html) shows how.

## Citation

There is no publication for dMod2 yet. The paper below describes [dMod](https://github.com/JetiLab/dMod), its predecessor, and is the reference for the modelling framework:

Kaschek D, Mader W, Fehling-Kaschek M, Rosenblatt M, Timmer J (2019). Dynamic Modeling, Parameter Estimation, and Uncertainty Analysis in R. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 88(10), 1-32. [doi:10.18637/jss.v088.i10](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v088.i10)
